draft.title: Allusion
card: An allusion is a brief reference to another text, person or event. The writer expects the reader to recognise it, so it is not explained.
Allusions often use a name, a phrase or an image. Calling a tough task a Herculean labour points to the myth of Hercules and his impossible tasks.
The effect is to add meaning in a few words. The reader brings what they know about the source to the new text.
An allusion only works if the reader knows the source. A reader who does not recognise it may miss the extra meaning.
draft.remember: An allusion is a short nod to a known source that adds meaning without explaining it.

a.q: Why does a writer use an allusion?
opts: To add meaning by pointing to a source the reader knows
To retell the whole of an earlier text in detail
To copy an earlier text so that it has the same setting
To explain a difficult idea step by step to the reader
a.why: An allusion is brief and relies on the reader recognising the source, so it adds meaning in few words. Retelling a text in detail is the opposite of a brief reference.
a.clue: Think about what the reader is expected to bring.

b.q: Mia writes in a blog post that the school hall felt like Pandora's box had been opened after the exam. Which statement best describes this line?
opts: It is an allusion that relies on the reader knowing the myth
It is a retelling of the myth set in a modern school
It is an allusion, but only if the myth is explained in full
It is a direct quote from the myth, used to prove a point
b.why: The line makes a brief reference to a well-known myth and expects the reader to recognise it. It does not retell the myth. The third option is tempting, but an allusion works without any explanation, so it does not need one.
b.clue: Is the myth told, or only pointed to?

a.best: To add meaning by pointing to a source the reader knows

b.best: It is an allusion that relies on the reader knowing the myth
